passages.happening:
God will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon (verse 1) and send winnowers to scatter her (verse 2). Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, though their land was full of guilt (verse 5).

“Flee from Babylon! Escape with your lives! Do not be destroyed in her punishment” (verse 6), for this is the time of the LORD's vengeance. ‘Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk’ (verse 7). ‘Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been shattered’ (verse 8). Her friends try to heal her, but she cannot be healed, so they leave her (verses 8 and 9). The LORD has brought out his people's vindication; they are to tell in Zion what he has done (verse 10).

The LORD has stirred up the kings of the Medes, for his purpose is to destroy Babylon, the vengeance for his temple (verse 11). ‘The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom’ (verse 15), and idols are a fraud (verses 17 and 18). Babylon was God's war club, with which he shattered nations, kingdoms and armies (verses 20 to 23). Now he will repay Babylon for all the evil she did in Zion (verse 24). He is against her, the destroying mountain, and will roll her down from the cliffs (verse 25).

The nations are called against her: Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz, and the kings of the Medes (verses 27 and 28). The land trembles. Babylon's warriors stop fighting and sit in their strongholds, and messenger after messenger runs to tell the king that his city is taken (verses 30 and 31). The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at treading time (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The Medes were an Iranian people whose kingdom had joined Babylon in destroying Nineveh in 612 BC. By the middle of the sixth century the Median kingdom had been absorbed by Cyrus of Persia, whose combined army took Babylon in 539 BC. Ararat is Urartu, around Lake Van in eastern Turkey; Minni and Ashkenaz were peoples of the mountains north of Mesopotamia.

The gold cup is a picture of Babylon's splendor used by God to make the nations drunk with judgment. The cup is beautiful, and it is still only a cup in God's hand.

Babylon's features appear all through the poem: its many waters, the Euphrates and a web of canals, and its thick walls. Babylon had been God's war club. Now the club is broken.

Verses 15 to 19 repeat almost word for word the hymn of 10:12-16. In the middle of the judgment on Babylon stands the praise of the God who made the earth.
passages.later: Revelation takes up the gold cup for the great city of its own vision, a woman holding ‘a golden cup full of abominations’ (Revelation 17:4). Isaiah heard the same news: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon!” (Isaiah 21:9).
passages.asks: Babylon was a gold cup in God's hand. Ask what great power or success you have mistaken for something that rules itself. And ask what it means that God's people were told to flee rather than fight.

passages.t: Zion's complaint, and come out of her
passages.happening:
Zion speaks. Nebuchadnezzar has devoured her, crushed her, swallowed her like a sea monster and spat her out (verse 34). Let the violence done to her be on Babylon, Jerusalem says (verse 35).

God answers that he will plead her case and take vengeance for her (verse 36). He will dry up Babylon's sea and make her springs run dry (verse 36). Babylon will become a heap of ruins (verse 37). He will make her officials and wise men drunk so they sleep and never wake (verse 39, 57). Sheshach is taken, the praise of the whole earth seized (verse 41). The sea rises over Babylon (verse 42). God will punish Bel in Babylon and make him spit out what he swallowed (verse 44).

“Come out of her, My people! Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD” (verse 45). They must not lose heart at rumors (verse 46). The days are coming when God will punish Babylon's idols, and heaven and earth will shout for joy over her (verses 47 and 48). As Babylon made Israel's slain fall, so Babylon's slain will fall (verse 49). Those who escaped the sword are to go and remember the LORD from far away and let Jerusalem come to mind (verse 50). Babylon's broad wall will be leveled and her high gates burned (verse 58).
passages.hearers:
Zion's complaint is the voice of a people whose temple was burned and whose children starved. The prophet lets that grief and anger speak to God instead of turning into private revenge.

Sheshach is again the code name for Babylon made by swapping letters of the alphabet from the end, as in 25:26.

Bel is Marduk, Babylon's god. The sea monster swallowed Zion, and now Bel must spit out what he swallowed: the captive people come home.

The command to God's people is to come out, not to fight. Vengeance belongs to God. The exiles are told to remember the LORD and Jerusalem from afar.
passages.later: Revelation quotes verse 45 for those who belong to God in the great city: “Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins” (Revelation 18:4). A psalm remembers Zion from the same rivers: ‘By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept’ (Psalm 137:1).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take the calls for Babylon's total destruction, including young men and whole armies?

The language is harsh, and readers should feel its weight. These are first the words of victims. Zion's complaint in verses 34 and 35 is the voice of a people whose temple was burned and whose children starved, and the prophets let that grief speak to God rather than turn into private revenge. The vengeance belongs to God; the people are told to flee, not to fight (verses 6, 45 and 50). And the images are the conventional language of ancient war oracles, which described defeat in total terms; Babylon was not in fact massacred in 539 BC. Some interpreters stress that the poem is about the end of an empire's power, not a plan for slaughter. Others add that the New Testament, which takes up this language in Revelation, leaves judgment to God and calls believers to love their enemies.

These words concern an ancient empire. These notes draw no line from them to any nation or state of the present day, and they give no one a warrant for violence against any people.
passages.asks: God's people were told to come out of Babylon and remember Jerusalem from afar. Ask what you need to come out of so that you do not share in its sins. And ask how you bring your anger at injustice to God instead of acting on it yourself.

passages.t: The scroll sunk in the Euphrates
passages.happening:
This is the message Jeremiah gave to Seraiah son of Neriah, the quartermaster, when he went to Babylon with King Zedekiah in the fourth year of his reign (verse 59). Jeremiah had written on one scroll all the disaster that would come on Babylon (verse 60).

He tells Seraiah that when he gets to Babylon, he is to read all these words aloud (verse 61) and say that the LORD has spoken against this place, to cut it off so that nothing lives in it (verse 62). ‘When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates’ (verse 63). Then he is to say that Babylon will sink like this and never rise again, because of the disaster God will bring on her (verse 64).

‘Here end the words of Jeremiah’ (verse 64).
passages.hearers:
The fourth year of Zedekiah is about 594 or 593 BC, the year envoys from the neighboring kingdoms met in Jerusalem to plan revolt. Zedekiah may have gone to Babylon to assure Nebuchadnezzar of his loyalty.

Seraiah son of Neriah was Baruch's brother, a high official who travelled with the king. So the book's last sign is carried out by the brother of the scribe who wrote it down.

The word against Babylon was written while Babylon was at the height of its power and Judah had not yet fallen. A scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the river was an acted sign: as it sinks, so will Babylon.

The chapter ends, here end the words of Jeremiah. Chapter 52 is a historical appendix.
passages.later: Revelation pictures the same sign for its great city: ‘a mighty angel picked up a stone the size of a great millstone and cast it into the sea’ (Revelation 18:21). Baruch, Seraiah's brother, had written Jeremiah's words (Jeremiah 36:4).
passages.asks: Jeremiah's word against Babylon was carried right into Babylon at the height of its power. Ask whether you believe God's word against a power that looks permanent. And ask what it means that the prophet's last act was a sign of hope for the exiles.
